hook: You know “Be still, and know that I am God”. But did you know it is spoken over raging nations and broken weapons?
known: Many people turn to this verse for calm, as an invitation to rest in God’s presence.
who: God. The psalm quotes him directly in this verse, and the singers answer in the next.
audience: In the verse’s own words, the nations and the earth: “I will be exalted among the nations. I will be exalted on the earth.”
setting: A song about God as a refuge when everything shakes: mountains fall into the sea, nations rage and kingdoms are moved.
around: The verse before it describes what God does: “He makes wars cease to the end of the earth. He breaks the bow, and shatters the spear.” The psalm opens with the confidence it ends on: “God is our refuge and strength”.
point: “Be still” is first a command to stop fighting and to recognize who God is. The rest it gives his people follows from that: the one who ends wars is their refuge.
story:
This psalm was not written for a quiet afternoon. It is a song for the day the ground gives way: “though the earth changes, though the mountains are shaken into the heart of the seas”.

Almost five hundred years ago, between 1527 and 1529, the reformer Martin Luther turned it into a hymn. In English it is called A Mighty Fortress Is Our God, and it has been known ever since as the battle hymn of the Reformation.

That name fits the psalm. When God says “Be still”, he is not speaking into silence. He is speaking into the noise of nations and armies, and telling everyone within earshot who is God. The stillness his people find there is the stillness of a refuge in a storm.
